entry: English rock band formed in London in 1988. Its debut album, *Leisure* (1991), drew on Madchester and shoegaze. Following a stylistic change influenced by British guitar pop, the albums *Modern Life Is Rubbish* (1993) and *Parklife* (1994) helped popularize Britpop. A 1995 chart battle with [[Oasis (band)|Oasis]], dubbed "the Battle of Britpop," aided the band's mass popularity in the U.K. The self-titled album of 1997 produced "Song 2," which became popular on U.S. alternative radio. Blur reunited in 2009 and released *The Ballad of Darren* in 2023.

American former professional baseball and football player. He is the only professional athlete to have been named an All-Star in two major American sports. At Auburn University he won the Heisman Trophy in 1985. He played in the [[National Football League|NFL]] for the Los Angeles Raiders and in [[Major League Baseball]] for the Kansas City Royals, Chicago White Sox, and California Angels. A 1991 hip injury ended his football career. The Nike "Bo Knows" advertising campaign of 1989 and 1990 made his name known beyond sports.

Roughly spherical region of space in the vicinity of the constellation Boötes. It contains just 60 [[Galaxy|galaxies]], far fewer than the approximately 2,000 expected for an area of comparable size. With a radius of 62 megaparsecs (nearly 200 million [[Light-year|light-years]]), it is one of the largest known voids in the visible universe. Astronomer Robert Kirshner discovered it in 1981 during a [[Redshift|redshift]] survey of galaxies. Its center lies 700 million light-years from Earth.

Watercraft of many types and sizes, generally smaller than a [[Ship|ship]]. Small boats are typically used on [[River|rivers]] and [[Lake|lakes]] or in protected coastal areas, while some, such as whaleboats, were built for offshore use. [[Submarine|Submarines]] are called boats regardless of size. A boat differs from a raft by obtaining [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]] from a waterproof structure, such as the planks of a wooden hull. Boats are propelled by manpower, wind, or inboard and outboard motors. The earliest known plank-built boats come from the Nile, dating to the third millennium BC. The oldest recovered boat, the Pesse [[Canoe|canoe]], is a dugout found in the [[Netherlands]] and dated to between 8200 and 7600 BC.

American media personality, game show host, and [[Animal rights|animal rights]] advocate. He hosted [[CBS]]'s *The Price Is Right* from 1972 to 2007, the longest-running game show in North American television history. He also hosted *Truth or Consequences* from 1956 to 1975. Barker joined the United States Navy Reserve during [[World War II]]. He supported animal rights groups such as People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. He retired from *The Price Is Right* in 2007.

American singer-songwriter, born Robert Allen Zimmerman. He rose to prominence in the early 1960s New York folk scene after moving to [[New York City]] in 1961. Songs such as "Blowin' in the Wind" (1963) became anthems of the civil rights and antiwar movements. His use of electric instrumentation on *Highway 61 Revisited* (1965) and the single "Like a Rolling Stone" (1965) provoked controversy and broadened his appeal into rock. After a 1966 motorcycle crash he stopped touring for seven years. *Time Out of Mind* (1997) won the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Album of the Year. He received a special [[Pulitzer Prize]] citation in 2008 and the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature "for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition." An estimated 125 million of his records have sold worldwide.

American choreographer, dancer, and director. Arguably the most influential figure in [[Jazz dance|jazz dance]] in the 20th century, he developed a style marked by finger-snapping, tilted bowler hats, turned-in knees, and jazz hands. He won nine Tony Awards, beginning with his choreography for *The Pajama Game* (1954). His film *Cabaret* (1972) won him the Academy Award for Best Director, and *All That Jazz* (1979) won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. His other works include the musicals *Sweet Charity* (1966) and *Chicago* (1975). His third wife, actor–dancer Gwen Verdon, collaborated with him on several theater and film projects.

British-born American comedian, actor, and entertainer. His career spanned nearly 80 years in [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]], radio, film, and television. He appeared in more than 70 short and feature films, including seven *Road to...* musical comedies with [[Bing Crosby]]. He hosted the [[Academy Awards]] ceremony a record 19 times. Between 1941 and 1991 he made 57 tours for the United Service Organizations (USO), entertaining military personnel around the world. In 1997 Congress made him an honorary veteran of the Armed Forces.

English actor and film director. Known for intense but sensitive portrayals of "tough guy" characters, he broke through as Arthur Parker in the BBC serial *Pennies from Heaven* (1978). *Mona Lisa* (1986) won him a BAFTA, a Golden Globe, and a [[Cannes Film Festival]] Best Actor award, and earned him an Academy Award nomination. He played the detective Eddie Valiant in *Who Framed Roger Rabbit* (1988). Hoskins also directed two features, *The Raggedy Rawney* (1988) and *Rainbow* (1996). He retired in 2012 owing to [[Parkinson's disease]].

Jamaican reggae singer, songwriter, and guitarist. Considered one of the pioneers of [[Reggae|reggae]], he became a global symbol of Jamaican music, culture, and identity. He became a [[Rastafari|Rastafarian]] icon, and his music reflected a strong sense of spirituality. After forming a group with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer that became the Wailers, he signed with Island Records; the albums *Catch a Fire* and *Burnin'* (both 1973) brought the group international attention. A live version of "No Woman, No Cry" (1975) became his first hit outside Jamaica, following the popularity of [[Eric Clapton]]'s version of "I Shot the Sheriff." In 1976 he survived an assassination attempt at his home in Jamaica. The compilation *Legend* (1984) became the best-selling reggae album of all time, with estimated sales of more than 75 million records worldwide.

American comedian and actor. Known for his deadpan, stammering delivery, he came to prominence in 1960 with the comedy album *The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart*, which reached number one on the Billboard pop album chart and won two [[Grammy Awards]]. He starred as psychologist Bob Hartley in *The Bob Newhart Show* (1972–1978) and as innkeeper Dick Loudon in *Newhart* (1982–1990). From 2013 to 2018 he played Professor Proton on [[The Big Bang Theory]], earning his first career Emmy Award.

American painter and art instructor. He created and hosted *The Joy of Painting*, an instructional program that aired from 1983 to 1994 on [[PBS]] in the United States. Its landscapes were painted quickly in [[Oil painting|oil]] by the wet-on-wet method with a limited palette. Ross, who had served in the United States Air Force, retired in 1981 and, with help from Annette Kowalski and her husband, set up Bob Ross Inc. The company later became the legal proprietor of his name and likeness.

American singer, songwriter, and actor, born Walden Robert Cassotto. He wrote and recorded the million-selling single "Splish Splash" (1958), followed by "Dream Lover" and "Mack the Knife." "Mack the Knife" won Record of the Year at the second annual [[Grammy Awards]], and Darin was the first winner of the Best New Artist award. A Golden Globe followed for his first film, *Come September*. In the 1960s he worked on the presidential campaign of [[Robert F. Kennedy]]. Long affected by a weak heart, he died after open-heart surgery in Los Angeles.

American chess grandmaster and the eleventh World Chess Champion. A [[Chess|chess]] prodigy, he won a record eight U.S. Championships, the first at age 14. In 1964 he won the U.S. Championship with an 11–0 score, the only perfect score in that tournament's history. In 1972 he defeated Boris Spassky of the U.S.S.R. in [[Reykjavík]], Iceland, in a match publicized as a [[Cold War]] confrontation. In 1975 he refused to defend the title after a dispute with FIDE, and Anatoly Karpov was named champion by default. Fischer later won an unofficial 1992 rematch against Spassky in Yugoslavia, which was under a [[United Nations]] embargo. He was arrested in Japan in 2004 for using a passport the U.S. had revoked, and was later granted Icelandic citizenship. His later public statements included [[Antisemitism|antisemitic]] remarks.

Medium-sized wild cat (*Lynx rufus*) native to North America. It is one of four extant species in the genus [[Lynx|Lynx]], and it ranges from southern [[Canada]] through most of the contiguous United States to [[Oaxaca]] in [[Mexico]]. It reaches up to 125 cm (50 in) in total length, including the tail. Bobcats hunt mainly [[Rabbit|rabbits]] and [[Hare|hares]], as well as rodents, birds, and [[Deer|deer]]. Listed as Least Concern by the IUCN since 2002, the species is stable, though its populations are declining in some areas.

Winter sport of timed speed runs down banked, iced tracks in gravity-powered sleds, ridden by teams of two to four athletes. Bobsleds were first built in the late 19th century in St. Moritz, Switzerland, by wealthy tourists who adapted delivery sleds and toboggans. These early sleds evolved into bobsleighs, [[Luge|luges]], and skeletons. Racing through St. Moritz's streets caused collisions, and bobsledding was eventually banned from public highways. The Cresta Run there remains the oldest in the world. The four-man event has been held at almost every [[Winter Olympic Games|Winter Games]] since 1924, the exception being 1960 in Squaw Valley, California. The two-man event was added in 1932 and the women's monobob in 2022. The International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation governs the sport.

Semi-legendary [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] monk traditionally credited with transmitting Chan (Zen) Buddhism to [[China]]. Little contemporary biographical information survives, and later accounts are layered with legend. Chinese sources describe him as coming from the Western Regions, a term that can mean Central Asia or the Indian subcontinent. He is regarded as the first Chinese patriarch of Chan. The 952 *Anthology of the Patriarchal Hall* lists him as the 28th patriarch in a line extending back to the Buddha. His teachings center on meditation and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. He is also popularly regarded as the founder of Shaolin kung fu, an idea popularized in the 20th century.

Mental disorder characterized by an overwhelming preoccupation with a perceived flaw in one's physical appearance. Also called dysmorphophobia, it is placed within the [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive–compulsive]] spectrum by the DSM-5. It affects up to 2–3% of the population, usually beginning in adolescence and affecting men and women at roughly similar rates. Sufferers often check and compare the flaw repetitively and avoid social contact that exposes it. Muscle dysmorphia, in which the body is perceived as too small, affects mostly men. The disorder is commonly underdiagnosed and carries high rates of suicidal thoughts.

Type of [[Nonverbal communication|nonverbal communication]] in which physical behaviors, rather than words, convey information. Such behavior includes facial expressions, body posture, gestures, eye movement, touch, and the use of space. Most of it occurs without conscious awareness, and it often complements verbal communication. Some researchers conclude that nonverbal communication accounts for the majority of information transmitted in interpersonal interactions. Interpretation varies across cultures, although societies generally agree on the meanings of specific behaviors. Whether body language is universal is debated. Unlike [[Sign language|sign languages]], it is not a true language. The study of body language is known as kinesics.

Wingless, blood-feeding [[Louse|louse]] that exclusively infests humans. Also called the clothing louse, it lives mainly in the seams of clothing and feeds on blood several times a day. Body lice cannot jump or fly, and spread by direct contact or through infested clothing and bedding. They transmit epidemic typhus, trench fever, and louse-borne relapsing fever. These pathogens have caused devastating outbreaks, including millions of deaths in World Wars I and II. Infestations occur where overcrowding, poor hygiene, and a lack of clean clothing prevail, such as in prisons, refugee camps, and homeless populations. Control relies on washing clothes and bedding in hot water of at least 54°C (130°F) and on delousing treatments.

Value (BMI) derived from a person's mass and height, used to categorize body weight. It is calculated as body mass in [[Kilogram|kilograms]] divided by the square of body height in square metres. Adult categories are underweight (under 18.5), normal weight (18.5 to 24.9), overweight (25 to 29.9), and [[Obesity|obese]] (30 or more). Originally called the Quetelet Index, it was devised in the 1830s by Adolphe Quetelet to describe populations rather than individuals. BMI does not distinguish lean mass from fat mass, so it may misclassify muscular athletes as overweight. Values under 20 and over 25 have been associated with higher all-cause mortality.

Deliberate alteration of the human anatomy or physical appearance. In its broadest sense it includes [[Tattoo|tattooing]], [[Body piercing|piercing]], scarification, branding, and subdermal implants, as well as religious rites of passage such as [[Circumcision|circumcision]] in some cultures. It is performed for reasons including [[Aesthetics|aesthetics]], group affiliation, remembrance, and self-expression. Such practices have persisted for millennia, with prehistoric origins in rituals marking status and identity. Health risks include bacterial infection, allergic reactions, scarring, and, when procedures are not sterile, bloodborne infections such as hepatitis.

Significant accumulation of water on Earth's surface. The term most often refers to [[Ocean|oceans]], [[Sea|seas]], and [[Lake|lakes]], but includes smaller pools such as ponds and [[Wetland|wetlands]], and flowing water such as [[River|rivers]] and canals. Most are natural, although most [[Reservoir|reservoirs]] are created by engineering [[Dam|dams]]. Bodies of water that are navigable are known as waterways. Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth's surface and hold approximately 96.5 percent of its water volume. [[Climate change]] is altering water bodies through rising temperatures, changed precipitation, and sea-level rise, while freshwater bodies face more frequent droughts.

Form of [[Body modification|body modification]] that punctures or cuts the body to insert jewelry or implants. Ear and nose piercing are the most widespread. The oldest mummified remains ever discovered had earrings, and nose piercing is documented from 1500 BCE. Nipple piercing dates back at least to [[Ancient Rome]], and genital piercing is described in ancient India, c. 320–550 CE. The practice waxed and waned in the West, then rose in popularity after [[World War II]] and spread into the mainstream in the 1990s. Motives include religious belief, self-expression, aesthetics, and rebellion, and some piercings have been restricted by schools and employers. Risks include allergic reaction, [[Infection|infection]], and scarring; healing can take a month for some genital piercings or up to two years for the navel.

Practice of progressive [[Exercise|resistance exercise]] to build, control, and develop muscles through hypertrophy. In competition, bodybuilders are judged on conditioning, muscularity, size, symmetry, and posing. Before contests they reduce body fat, and in the final stage they use [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrate]] loading and dehydration to maximize definition. A novice may gain 8–15 pounds (4–7 kg) of muscle per year lifting weights for seven hours per week, though gains slow after two years. Some bodybuilders use anabolic steroids, which carry serious health risks and are prohibited by most competitions. The NABBA Universe Championships, considered the top amateur contests since 1950, have had winners including [[Ronnie Coleman]] and [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]].
